## Guess first

Let's say we had **\$500,000** and we want to spend **\$20,000** a year. Well,
then we know that in 25 years we'll run out of money. It'll all be gone.

We've also heard of interest. If we put the \$500,000 in a bank, we'll get
some more money every year. So what if we were to make **2%** interest every
year? Will the money last longer than 25 years, if we spend \$20,000 a year?

Now, another thing that happens over the years, especially over, say, 25
years, is that things get more expensive. 25 years ago, a meal probably cost a
lot less. You could probably get french fries and a hamburger for \$5, and
today that might cost \$10. If you are buying hamburgers, you may have to
spend more each year. That's called **inflation**.

But you might be getting money from interest, and the money you get from
interest might be a little more than the money you have to spend from
inflation. Suppose your money earns 5% interest and there's 4% inflation. Then
in a real sense you're getting **1%** more value per year. So how does that
affect how long the money will last?

Remember, in this second part you're not spending \$20,000 a year. You're
spending \$20,000 *worth* every year, based on the first year's prices.

Write your guesses down before reading on. Nobody will check them. That's the point.

## Meet the man who asked first

![Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci. The picture is from 1850, so it's a bit of a guess what he might have looked like. (Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.)](media/261102.moneymath.fibonacci-portrait.jpg){width=45% fig-align="center"}

Most people know Fibonacci for coming up with a sequence where you take the
two previous numbers and add them. You might start with 1, 1. Add them, you
get 2. Then you add the two previous ones: 1 plus 2 is 3, 2 plus 3 is 5. So
the Fibonacci sequence is 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, …

It has a lot of interesting history and all kinds of deep connections. It
connects out to something called the golden ratio, which is what makes certain
things look very aesthetic. They say the Parthenon follows the golden ratio in
terms of its height versus its width. I'm not sure why, but that's what I've
found out.

But what's interesting here is his *Liber Abaci* ("The Book of Calculation").
He wrote it in 1202, so this is a long time ago. It was where he showed
merchants, Italian merchants, how to use Hindu–Arabic numerals to find
profits, convert money from one country's currency to another's, and work out
interest. And interest is what we're looking at here.

Somewhere in there is a problem that's basically ours: someone has money in
the bank and takes a fixed amount out each year. When does it run out?

## Build it in a spreadsheet

[Download the spreadsheet](media/261102.moneymath.how-long.xlsx){download="how-long.xlsx"}.

Click on the spreadsheet and see how your guess works out.

What's great about a spreadsheet is that it's a table, but you can change the
numbers at the top. What if you start with \$100,000 instead of \$500,000?
What if you start with \$100? What if you were getting more interest? What if
you're getting less interest? You can change all the numbers at the top, and
the great thing about spreadsheets is that everything changes. It lets you see
when it turns red, when the money would run out. And if you actually spend
less or get more interest, you might never run out of money, which is a good
thing.

The yellow cells are the inputs. Each row is one year:

| year | start balance | + interest | − spending | end balance |
|------|---------------|------------|------------|-------------|
| 1 | 500,000 | 5,000 | 20,000 | 485,000 |
| 2 | 485,000 | 4,850 | 20,000 | 469,850 |
| … | | | | |

Now try these:

- Change spending to \$25,000. What happens?
- Change it to \$5,000. What happens now? (Don't skip this one.)
- What's the *most* you can spend so that the money **never** runs out?

## The pattern

At \$5,000 a year the balance never moves, because you're spending exactly the
interest (1% of \$500,000 = \$5,000). Spend less than the interest and the pile
grows forever. Spend more and it shrinks, and it shrinks *faster* each year,
because a smaller pile earns less interest. That's why the last few years of
the spreadsheet drop so steeply.

::: {.callout-note .lvl1 title="Percentages · Try it"}
Your spreadsheet has a "Continuous formula" cell up top that says the money
lasts about **28.8 years**. Your table ran out in **year 29**. Two completely
different methods agree. Whenever two methods agree, you can trust both a bit
more. You'll use this trick all through the book.
:::

::: {#box-logs .callout-note .lvl2 collapse="true" title="Logarithms · a formula instead of a table"}
The table works, but it takes 29 rows. The shortcut needs two functions from
precalculus.

The exponential is one of the most important functions in business because it
represents continuously compounded return

$$
FV = PV e^{rt}
$$

We begin with logarithms, which are the inverse of the exponential. In this
course, just like we use $e$ as the default base for an exponential function,
we use the natural log $\ln$ as the default logarithm.

With those two, the table collapses into one line:

$$
T = \frac{1}{r}\,\ln\!\frac{c}{c - rW}
$$

where $W$ is the nest egg, $c$ is yearly spending and $r$ is the interest rate
(as a decimal). With our numbers, $T = 100 \ln(20000/15000) \approx 28.8$ years.

Notice what happens when $c = rW$ (spending equals interest): the bottom of
the fraction is zero, and the formula says "forever". That's the pattern you
found in the spreadsheet.

Here's the same thing in Python, checked against the year-by-year method:

::: {#cf59d30c .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from math import log

W0, c, r = 500_000, 20_000, 0.01

# year by year, like the spreadsheet
W, years = W0, 0
while W > 0:
    W = W * (1 + r) - c
    years += 1

T = log(c / (c - r * W0)) / r      # the shortcut formula
print(f"year by year: runs out during year {years}")
print(f"formula:      T = {T:.1f} years")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
year by year: runs out during year 29
formula:      T = 28.8 years
```
:::
:::

::: {#box-softmax .callout-note .lvl2 collapse="true" title="Softmax · how a chatbot turns scores into odds"}

A chatbot writes one token at a time. At each step it gives every token in its
dictionary a **score**: bigger means "more likely to come next". Scores can be
any number, even negative, so they aren't probabilities yet.

To turn scores into probabilities it uses the same $e$ as continuous
compounding. Raise $e$ to each score, then divide by the total:

$$
p_i = \frac{e^{s_i}}{\sum_j e^{s_j}}
$$

This is called **softmax**. The exponential makes every number positive, and
dividing by the total makes them add up to 1. And just as compounding turns a
small difference in interest rate into a big difference in money, the
exponential turns a small lead in score into a big lead in probability: a
score 1 higher means $e \approx 2.7$ times as likely.

Here the model has just written *"The money will last 28."* and is choosing
the next token:

::: {#c0eb366b .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from math import exp

scores = {"8": 3.0, "9": 2.0, "7": 1.0, "5": -1.0}   # made-up scores

total = sum(exp(s) for s in scores.values())
probs = {tok: exp(s) / total for tok, s in scores.items()}
for tok, p in probs.items():
    print(f"'{tok}': {p:.3f}")

# second check: probabilities add to 1, and a score 1 higher is e times as likely
print(f"sum = {sum(probs.values()):.6f}")
print(f"p('8') / p('9') = {probs['8'] / probs['9']:.4f}  vs  e = {exp(1):.4f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
'8': 0.657
'9': 0.242
'7': 0.089
'5': 0.012
sum = 1.000000
p('8') / p('9') = 2.7183  vs  e = 2.7183
```
:::
:::


So the model will most likely write "28.8", but about one time in four it
writes "28.9", which is where the confident-but-wrong answers come from. Some
chatbots let you set a **temperature**: dividing every score by a number
bigger than 1 flattens the differences, so the model takes more chances.

::: {#box-series .callout-note .lvl2 collapse="true" title="Series · why the table has a formula at all"}
Each year the money you still have grows by a factor of $1.01$, and another
\$20,000 comes out. Add up all those withdrawals and their lost interest and
you get a geometric series.

A series is the sum of a sequence --- an infinite sum. The sum of an infinite
list of numbers can either be finite, so the series can *converge* to a
number, or the sum can be infinite, so the series *diverges*.

We start with the basic geometric series:

$$S = 1+r+r^2+r^3+r^4+\cdots$$

Here $r$ is a constant, the series converges when $|r|<1$ and diverges when
$1\leq|r|$. In fact, we can find what number the infinite geometric series
converges to. Write the series out for $Sr$:

$$Sr = r+r^2+r^3+r^4+r^5+\cdots$$

Looks a lot like the series for $S$ itself. Now subtract:

$$S-Sr=1$$

All the terms cancel! And then solve for $S$:

$$S=\frac1{1-r}=1+r+r^2+r^3+r^4+\cdots$$

Now that we know $S$, we can easily find other finite sums like

$$1+r+r^2+\cdots+r^{321}=S-Sr^{322}=S(1-r^{322})=\frac{1-r^{322}}{1-r}$$

For the money, the ratio is $1.01$ instead of $r$, and we stop after $n$ years
instead of going on forever. Set the balance to zero and solve for $n$:

$$
n = \frac{\ln\big(c/(c - rW)\big)}{\ln(1+r)} = \frac{\ln(4/3)}{\ln 1.01} \approx 28.9 \text{ years,}
$$

which matches the spreadsheet (year 29) even better than the continuous 28.8.

::: {#box-sim .callout-note .lvl2 collapse="true" title="Simulation · what if returns are random?"}
Real investments don't pay a steady 1%. Some years are great, some are
terrible. Let's say returns average 3% but swing a lot, then simulate
10,000 possible futures and count how many run out within 30 years:

::: {#24b5f0f6 .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n, years = 10_000, 30
returns = rng.normal(0.03, 0.12, size=(n, years))

W = np.full(n, 500_000.0)
paths = np.empty((n, years))
for t in range(years):
    W = np.maximum(W * (1 + returns[:, t]) - 20_000, 0)
    paths[:, t] = W

print(f"ran out within {years} years: {(paths[:, -1] == 0).mean():.1%}")

plt.plot(paths[:50].T / 1000, lw=0.7, alpha=0.6)
plt.xlabel("year"); plt.ylabel("balance ($ thousands)")
plt.title("50 of the 10,000 simulated futures");
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
ran out within 30 years: 36.5%
```
:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](moneymath-how-long_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-2.png){width=604 height=450}
:::
:::


The average return (3%) is *higher* than before, yet about a third of the futures
still run dry. Bad years early on hurt the most, because they shrink the pile
right when it has the most growing left to do.

::: {#box-diffeq .callout-note .lvl3 collapse="true" title="Differential equations · where the formula comes from"}
Treat time as continuous. The balance changes at the rate *interest in minus
spending out*:

$$
\frac{dW}{dt} = rW - c, \qquad W(0) = W_0 .
$$

That's a differential equation.

If $f(x)$ is a function, then $f'(x)$ or $df/dx$ is its derivative. We can
make equations involving them. In these equations, we *solve for $f(x)$*
using integration. We can also plug in functions by taking their derivatives
to see whether they satisfy a differential equation.

For instance, we can look at the equation $f' = k f$, and then we can try
$f=\cos(x)$. Then $f'(x)=-\sin(x)$, so when we plug in we get
$\cos(x)=-k\sin(x)$. *These are unequal* so $f=\cos(x)$ does not solve the
equation. Next we can try $f=e^{kx}$ so that $f'=k e^{kx}$. Plugging in we get
$ke^{kx}=k e^{kx}$ so that $f=e^{kx}$ does solve the equation.

Our money equation is almost $f' = kf$, just with the $-c$ tacked on. So try
an exponential plus a constant, and plug in. It works:

$$
W(t) = \frac{c}{r} + \left(W_0 - \frac{c}{r}\right)e^{rt}.
$$

Set $W(T) = 0$ and solve for $T$ to get the logarithm formula. The quantity
$c/r$ is the balance whose interest exactly pays for the spending: start above
it and you grow forever, start below it and you hit zero.

**Your spreadsheet was solving this equation all along.**

![Leonhard Euler in 1753, pastel by Jakob Emanuel Handmann. He had already lost the sight of his right eye in the late 1730s, and went on to publish more mathematics than almost anyone in history. (Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.)](media/261102.moneymath.euler-portrait.jpg){width=35% fig-align="center"}

A differential equation $y'(x)=f(x,y)$ specifies the slope of a solution curve
$y(x)$ at any point $(x,y)$ in the plane. Suppose we want to estimate the
solution $y(x)$ with a given initial value $y(x_0)=y_0$. This can be done more
simply by realizing that the slope is the "rise-over-run", so the
$\Delta y = f(x,y)\Delta x$ is how much the $y$ increases when we take a step
$\Delta x$.

For us $f = rW - c$ and the step is one year, so $\Delta W = rW - c$:
interest minus spending, which is exactly one row of the spreadsheet. The
29-row table is Euler's method with $\Delta t = 1$. That's why it lands close
to, but not exactly on, the continuous answer of 28.8 years.

The random version, where returns are noisy and your lifetime is uncertain
too, is Milevsky's seventh equation, named for Andrey Kolmogorov. It gives the
probability of outliving your money.

::: {#box-adds .callout-note .lvl3 collapse="true" title="Interpretability · watching a model add"}

Can we look inside a model and see *how* it does a sum? A new field called
**interpretability** tries to do exactly that. Researchers trace which parts
of the model light up, and what each part contributes, as it works.

In 2025, researchers at Anthropic traced one of their models adding
$36 + 59$. It didn't carry the one. It ran two paths side by side:

- one path made a **rough estimate** of the size, something like "a bit over
  90";
- another worked out **only the last digit** exactly: 6 + 9 ends in 5.

Put together, "a bit over 90" and "ends in 5" give **95**. That's a strange
way to add, but it works, and nobody taught it that. It found the method on its
own while learning to predict text.

Here's the part worth remembering. When they then asked the model *how* it got
95, it described the school method: add the ones, carry the one, add the tens.
Its explanation was a sensible story, but it wasn't what it had actually done.

So checking a chatbot means checking two things: its **answer** (against your
spreadsheet) and its **explanation** (which may be a plausible story rather
than a report).

## Using AI

Ask an AI assistant: *"I have \$500,000, spend \$20,000 a year and earn 1%.
How many years will it last?"*

Then **check** its answer against your spreadsheet. AI chatbots are often
shaky at arithmetic, even when they sound very sure of themselves. If it's
wrong, can you work out what it did? Now ask it to *write a spreadsheet
formula or Python code* for the problem instead of answering directly, and
check that. Which way worked better?

### What the chatbot sees

When you type *"I have \$500,000"*, the chatbot never sees the number the way
you do. Before anything else happens, your text is chopped into **tokens**:
short chunks that the model has a numbered list of, a bit like a dictionary
where every entry has a page number. The model only ever sees the page
numbers.

Long numbers usually get chopped too. Many chatbots cut digits into chunks of
up to three, so 500,000 might arrive as `500` · `,` · `000`: three tokens, and
nothing in them says "this `500` means five hundred *thousand*". You learned
place value in second grade. The model has to work it out from patterns in
everything it read.

That's one reason a chatbot can explain compound interest beautifully and
still get the arithmetic wrong. Explaining is about patterns in words, which
is what it's built for. Arithmetic is about place value, which it never sees
directly.

## Open question

The simulation stops at 30 years. But how long will *you* live? That's a
probability question too, and it has its own equation (and its own slightly
morbid spreadsheet). Next chapter.
